etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English porche, from Old French, from Latin porticus (“portico”). Doublet of portego, portico, and porticus.

definitions.definition: (architecture) A covered entrance to a building, whether taken from the interior, and forming a sort of vestibule within the main wall, or projecting without and with a separate roof. A porch often has chair(s), table(s) and swings.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter V, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: But Miss Thorn relieved the situation by laughing aloud, […] . We began to tell her about Mohair and the cotillon, and of our point of observation from the Florentine galleried porch, and she insisted she would join us there.

definitions.definition: The platform outside the external hatch of a spacecraft.

quote.citation: 2012, Courtney G. Brooks, James M. Grimwood, Loyd S. Swenson, Chariots for Apollo:
quote.text: By the time he had put on the backpack, McDivitt was ready to let him do more—to stand on the porch at least.
